extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of Plato/Republic; undergraduate philosophy readers
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and prescriptive account of how to educate, select, and prepare philosopher‑kings in Plato's Republic, including curriculum, stages, character traits, and political implications. Focuses on the sequence from bodily training through mathematics to dialectic and the practical return to political life.

rubrics_metrics.name: State purpose: citizens serve common good
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose in framing the State was not that our citizens should do what they like, but that they should serve the State for the common good of all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle justifies compelling those best fitted (philosophers) to rule rather than allowing personal preference to determine office; individual desire to avoid duty is not a valid reason to exempt someone from serving the common good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulers must not be desirous to rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who rule must not be those who are desirous to rule; the philosopher who would rather live in the heaven of ideas must be forced down again among the captives to partake of their labours and honours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosopher-rulers should be selected/trained so that they can govern disinterestedly — they should be willing to descend into practical life and use 'eyes in the dark' to see better than those who quarrel about shadows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary science: number/calculation as conductor to thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal or primary science of which all the arts and sciences are partakers is number or calculation; number is rather to be regarded as a conductor to thought and being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arithmetic is valued not for practical counting alone but as an abstract discipline that sharpens the intellect, provokes reflection on unity/plurality/relations, and elevates the mind out of sensory flux toward contemplation of being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum sequencing (gymnastic → music → mathematics → dialectic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Former education had two branches, gymnastic (body) and music (mind); beyond these proceed to number/arithmetic, then plane geometry, solid geometry, astronomy (solids in motion), harmonics, and finally dialectic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each stage is preparatory to the next: bodily training and literature form the base; mathematical studies 'play the prelude' and develop abstraction and order; dialectic is the 'hymn' or coping‑stone and must be pursued after earlier sciences to lead the mind to the idea of the good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical studies pursued in philosopher's spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics must be pursued in the spirit of a philosopher, not of a shopkeeper: concerned with abstract truth, not visible objects or mere action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematics should be treated as pure abstractions (e.g., the arithmetician's 'one' is indivisible); avoid treating geometry, astronomy, or harmonics as mere technical applications. Use problems and abstract analysis rather than empirical tinkering or commercial utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectic as the highest discipline leading to the idea of Good
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialectic is that science which defines and explains the essence or being of each nature, distinguishes and abstracts the good, and is ready to do battle against all opponents in the cause of good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialectic withdraws from sense to pure intellect, is the 'royal road' from the cave into light, and should only be taught after previous mathematical and preparatory studies; without dialectic the rulers would be intellectually inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria: intellectual and moral qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers must be constant and valiant, good-looking, of noble manners, quick at learning, capable of mental toil, retentive, solid, diligent natures who combine intellectual with moral virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude those 'lame and one-sided' (diligent in body but indolent in mind or vice versa), a 'maimed soul' (whose conduct contradicts stated principles), the 'bastard or feeble person'; candidates should be sound in wind and limb and in perfect condition for mental gymnastic trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age and staged timing of education and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Education and selection occur in stages: initial youth training (playful learning), selection at about twenty for promising disciples, further selection at thirty for those able to withdraw into abstraction, a second gymnastic of the soul for ~5–6 years beginning at thirty, fifteen years of public service, and return at fifty to pursue the idea of good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Youth should begin with play to detect bent; avoid exposing very young pupils to dialectic; prescribed ages and durations structure when to intensify philosophical instruction and when to gain practical experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature philosophical study for the young
rubrics_metrics.description: Young persons should not study philosophy too early: a young man is a sort of puppy who only plays with an argument and may be reasoned into and out of his opinions every day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early exposure to dialectic can unsettle firm principles, lead to scepticism, and discredit both the student and philosophy; delay serious dialectical training until maturity (~30) to prevent frivolous paradox‑pursuit and moral unsettlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematician versus dialectician distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The faculty of the mathematician is distinct from the higher philosophical sense (dialectic); 'I have hardly ever known a mathematician who could reason.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical skill sharpens and prepares the mind but is not equivalent to dialectical ability; educational programs must move beyond problem-solving to training in first principles and synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomy and harmonics: study abstractly by problems, not empirical star-gazing
rubrics_metrics.description: Star-gazing as ordinarily practised draws the soul 'downwards' — the magnificence of the heavens is the embroidery of a copy and teaches nothing about absolute harmonies; astronomy must be placed on a truly scientific basis by problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid empirical, sense-based astronomy or empiricist harmonics (twisting strings, auscultation); study mathematical problems and abstract numerical relations that point to universal relations, not mere sensory appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of women in education and rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Women will share in all things with the men; the governesses are part of the perfect image of the governors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational and civic roles (war and peace) are to be common to both sexes in the ideal State; training and duties should not be gender-exclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosopher-ruler character: despise earthly vanities and serve justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosopher-kings will despise earthly vanities and will be the servants of justice only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal ruler's motivation must be service to justice rather than personal or material ambition; such rulers may be honoured sacramentally but must govern according to the idea of the good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political suitability judged by ability to reconcile ideals and practical life
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegory of the cave implies two disorders of eyesight in statesmen: (1) those too given to general maxims or abstractions who cannot see present political realities; (2) those limited to their trade/class who see only near interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good political actors must avoid the extremes of abstract intoxication (theorists who cannot accommodate practical constraints) and parochial narrowness (craftsmen/politicians who lack universal perspective); training should cultivate both theoretical vision and practical competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of education: draw men from becoming to being; realize and connect abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: True education draws men from becoming to being; it develops the faculty of seeing the universal in all things and seeks to combine the universals disengaged from sense into a comprehensive survey of being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education should cultivate the power of abstraction and synthesis (while recognising later critics' cautions about 'mere abstractions'); the end goal is contemplation of the idea of the good and ordering life after that pattern.
